paras: The Huntsville election-day assault on Black voters was an attack on a line of Black men marching to the polls in Huntsville, Alabama, during the state election of August 1880. According to letters sent to Washington, a white Democrat clubbed the voters with a cane, severely wounding one man, striking several others and dispersing them. Republican papers in the North printed the letters as evidence that intimidation and fraud had produced the large Democratic majority in Alabama.

In Madison County, Republicans and Independents backed Harrison for probate judge on a 'combination' ticket against the Democratic candidate. Deputy marshal Hewlitt complained that the Democrats controlled the election machinery, rejecting the inspectors the opposition chose.

The polls in Huntsville opened at 7 o'clock, and soon afterward a brass band led a procession of colored voters described as 'under the control of friends of the Democrats' to the polling place. A second line of colored voters followed, shouting for Harrison. When they reached the voting place, an unnamed Republican eyewitness wrote, 'a young white man and Democrat named Tom Sprogins,' encouraged by 'the mob spirit of his friends,' attacked them. He knocked down and severely wounded one colored man with a cane, struck several others and dispersed the Harrison voters for a time.

Hewlitt's letter described the same scene as an assault by Democrats on Independent Republican voters at 'the Huntsville box,' in which one colored man was knocked down and others were assaulted with sticks and pistols. A Huntsville correspondent of the Indianapolis Sun, a Greenback paper, wrote that armed 'Bourbons' behind a brass band took possession of the polls, that several colored Greenback voters were driven off with clubs, and that 'pistols were drawn by the score.'

No report of an arrest or charge against Sprogins or anyone else was found in the coverage. The eyewitness letter and Hewlitt's letter were both sent to Gen. Raum, Commissioner of Internal Revenue, and released in Washington for publication. Hewlitt also reported that about 150 Democrats left Huntsville after the election with a small cannon, the 'little Democrat,' to celebrate in Madison, Triana and Whitesburg.

The episode reached print only through Republican papers outside the South, as part of a campaign against the Alabama result. The Wilmington Daily Republican first carried a paraphrase of the eyewitness letter under the headline 'Unblushing Frauds,' answering Senator Morgan's claim that the election had been fair, and the Burlington Free Press reprinted it. The Chicago Tribune quoted the letter in full the next day, naming Sprogins and calling the attack 'unprovoked.'

Hewlitt's letter ran in the New-York Tribune under 'How Alabama Was Carried' and was reprinted by the Chicago Tribune and the Wheeling Intelligencer. A Chicago Tribune editorial then joined it to the Sun letter, saying the two 'exactly' corroborated each other and blaming 'bulldozers' for the result. None of the papers named the injured man, and no Black-press coverage of the assault was found.

The Huntsville Independent, as quoted by Hewlitt, insisted that 'Peace prevailed in Madison last Monday' and that anyone alleging 'buldozen' lied. That denial was general rather than a reply to the specific charge, while the three accusing accounts all came from opponents of the Democratic ticket and differed on whether one man or a body of Democrats did the beating.

reader.title: Huntsville election-day assault on Black voters (1880)
bases: Three partisan letters describe white Democrats attacking a body of Black voters at the Huntsville polls with a cane, sticks or clubs, injuring at least one man and dispersing the rest (A3, A5, A7).

Three different letter-writers (an unnamed Republican, deputy marshal Hewlitt, and a Huntsville correspondent of the Indianapolis Sun) agree that Black voters were assaulted at the Huntsville polls on election day (A3, A5, A7); the only contrary statement is the Huntsville Independent's general denial of 'bulldozing,' quoted second-hand (A5).

accounts.label: Unnamed Alabama Republican (letter to Raum)
accounts.gist: An eyewitness wrote that after a band-led procession of Democratic-controlled colored voters, Tom Sprogins attacked the following line of Harrison voters, knocking one colored man down with a cane, severely wounding him, striking several others and dispersing them for a time.

accounts.label: Deputy marshal Hewlitt (letter to Raum)
accounts.gist: Democrats assaulted a number of Independent Republican voters at the Huntsville box; one colored man was knocked down and others were assaulted with sticks and pistols, intimidating them.

accounts.label: Huntsville correspondent of the Indianapolis Sun
accounts.gist: Bourbons led by a brass band and armed with sticks and pistols took possession of the polls; several colored men who came to vote the Greenback ticket were assaulted and driven off with clubs, and pistols were drawn.

accounts.label: Huntsville Independent (Democratic local paper, quoted)
accounts.gist: Peace prevailed in Madison on election day, and anyone who said there was bulldozing lied.

framing.detail: The Wilmington Daily Republican ran the paraphrase under 'Unblushing Frauds' as rebuttal to Senator Morgan's claim of a fair election.
The Chicago Tribune printed the letter as one of many showing 'intimidation and false counting,' calling the attack 'unprovoked.'
The New-York Tribune headlined Hewlitt's letter 'How Alabama Was Carried,' closing on 'the monumental fraud of the age.'
A Chicago Tribune editorial blamed 'bulldozers' and 'Bourbons' and said the Sun letter 'exactly corroborates' Hewlitt's charge.

record_check.dossier: Election day, 'last Monday' before Aug. 5, apparently 1880-08-02, shortly after 7 a.m.
Unnamed colored voters for Harrison (Republican/Independent/Greenback 'combination' ticket); none named.
Tom Sprogins, a young white Democrat, per one letter; Democrats/'Bourbons' as a group per two others.
Partisan crowd of Democrats (one named white assailant).
At least 1 severely wounded; several others struck or 'badly hurt'.
Beating with cane, sticks or clubs; pistols drawn; voters driven from the polls.
Seven articles in five white papers, Aug. 12-28, from three separate letters; no Black-press coverage found.
